response.title: Black Saturday: The Grounded Flight
response.immediate: At 12:04 p.m., General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs hand Kennedy a written objection: Air Force One cannot be launched unescorted into Cuban airspace without a filed flight plan, an identification arrangement with Havana, and a receiving field cleared to accept it. No such arrangements exist. The Andrews crew is put on standby and begins pre-flight checks, but the aircraft does not move from its hardstand. McNamara, given forty minutes, returns not with a flight authorization but with a substitute plan: ground the aircraft, intensify reconnaissance, and let RFK reopen the Dobrynin channel before any strike order is considered.
response.worldReaction: No word has reached Havana or Moscow of the proposed flight; it never left the ground, so there is nothing for Castro or Khrushchev to react to. Inside the Executive Committee, the effect is immediate: several members treat the episode as evidence the crisis is being run on nerve rather than method, and the room reconvenes divided — some backing the Chiefs' strike timetable, others insisting any Soviet offer must mean verified removal, not promises.
response.consequences: The flight proposal is set aside, not answered — Castro was never asked, Havana never cleared, no aircraft crossed the Straits. What remains open: whether Kennedy authorizes the Chiefs' OPLAN 312 timetable or extends the diplomatic pause; whether RFK is permitted to offer a binding non-invasion pledge to Dobrynin and how the Turkish missiles are handled in that offer; and how the quarantine line responds to the submarine now approaching it — surface it, let it pass, or escalate.
response.detailed:
Noon, the Cabinet Room, cigarette smoke thick over cold coffee. Kennedy's order to fly directly to Cuba is met first with silence, then with LeMay's flat refusal to treat it as executable: no flight plan filed, no Cuban air-defense coordination, no field designated to receive the aircraft, and no channel open to Castro to ask permission. The Chiefs put the objection on paper within the hour. Andrews Air Force Base holds Air Force One on alert status — engines checked, crew briefed — but issues no takeoff clearance pending a revised presidential order.

McNamara uses the interval to reframe the objective: keep the plane on the ground, widen the reconnaissance track over the missile sites, and let Robert Kennedy re-engage Dobrynin rather than stake the presidency on an unscheduled landing in hostile airspace. RFK does exactly that — reopening contact with the Soviet ambassador and indicating Washington will give a binding non-invasion guarantee if the missiles are removed and verified, while declining, for now, to put Turkey on the table publicly.

Meanwhile the Joint Chiefs deliver an expanded OPLAN 312 package — a strike sequence against the SAM batteries with named follow-on targets — and reiterate in writing that every day of delay increases the exposure of American reconnaissance pilots. LeMay works the corridors outside the formal session, arguing privately to fellow officers that the quarantine and negotiation have already failed. The Executive Committee reconvenes past 3 p.m. split along that line: strike now, or hold for what Dobrynin brings back. No word has come from Havana. No word has come from Moscow. The four-hour window closes with the aircraft still on the ground at Andrews.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I don't have a runway in Havana, I don't have a Cuban acknowledgment, and I don't have thirty minutes to invent either. I withdrew the flight order. What I have instead is Dobrynin, and RFK already back in that room. That's a channel with a return address. The tarmac isn't.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You want to land a president in a country that just shot down one of our pilots this morning. I put my objection on paper because someone has to. Every hour we spend on this instead of the strike package is an hour those SAM crews get better at killing our men. The Chiefs' plan is ready. It's the only thing in this building that is.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Castro isn't the man who ends this — Khrushchev is, and he's not going to hear about a plane landing in Havana before he hears from us through Dobrynin. I'm back in with the ambassador. We can put the non-invasion pledge on the table. Let's not hand LeMay an excuse to say diplomacy failed before it's even had the afternoon.

response.chronicleEntry: Kennedy ordered an unescorted presidential flight to Cuba to meet Castro; Joint Chiefs objected in writing, citing no flight plan, no Cuban clearance, and no contact with Castro. Air Force One held at Andrews, never cleared for takeoff. McNamara withdrew the flight order, proposing a diplomatic pause and intensified reconnaissance instead. RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel, offering a conditional binding non-invasion pledge in exchange for verified missile removal, while withholding public commitment on Turkey. The Joint Chiefs submitted an expanded OPLAN 312 strike timetable; LeMay lobbied officers privately for immediate strikes. The Executive Committee reconvened split between the strike timetable and the diplomatic pause, with the missile question and the approaching submarine still unresolved.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 shot down over Cuba, its pilot killed. Quarantine in force, no hotline to Moscow. Kennedy ordered an unescorted flight to Cuba to meet Castro directly; the Joint Chiefs objected in writing, citing no flight plan, no Cuban clearance, no Castro contact. The aircraft was held at Andrews. McNamara proposed grounding it, intensifying reconnaissance, and reopening the Dobrynin channel. RFK re-engaged Dobrynin, offering a binding non-invasion pledge for verified missile removal, withholding public commitment on Turkey. LeMay pressed for OPLAN 312 and lobbied officers privately. The Executive Committee split between striking now and awaiting Moscow's response. Missiles remain in Cuba, undestroyed and unverified as removed.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: At 1:40 p.m. Admiral Anderson relays the president's order through CINCLANT: destroyers hold quarantine stations but cease depth-charge signaling against the submerged contact. By late afternoon the Joint Chiefs enter formal objection in the record while complying. After nightfall, without further explosions near her hull, Captain Savitsky surfaces B-59 to ventilate and recharge batteries. USS Cony and Beale observe from station but do not fire, do not close, do not illuminate with searchlights. No shots exchanged. Kennedy is informed at 9:52 p.m. that the submarine is up and the destroyers are holding.
response.worldReaction: McNamara reports the immediate naval crisis eased but the missiles remain operational. LeMay circulates a memorandum renewing the unanimous Chiefs' recommendation for OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, arguing the submarine incident proves Soviet forces will test restraint, and requests final launch-readiness authority. RFK reopens the Dobrynin channel, indicating a non-invasion pledge is possible and probing whether Turkey can be handled privately. In Moscow, Khrushchev receives word the submarine surfaced unmolested and instructs the Washington channel to stay open, preparing to press public terms while reserving Turkey for private bargain.
response.consequences: Nothing further has been ordered. The Chiefs' request for launch-readiness authority sits unanswered on the Cabinet Room table. RFK has not been given authority to discuss Turkey, nor instructed which of Khrushchev's two term-sets to answer, nor by what channel. The quarantine's next posture — hold, tighten, or resume coercive signaling — is undecided. Whether Savitsky's report of American restraint reaches Moscow before Khrushchev finalizes his public message is unknown; it depends on Soviet naval communications procedure, not on anything Washington controls or can observe.
response.detailed:
1:40 p.m., 27 October. Kennedy's direction reaches Anderson at Atlantic Fleet headquarters: hold the quarantine line, stop harassing the submerged contact. Anderson objects on the record — the Chiefs have wanted depth charges as a signal, not a weapon, and now that tool is gone — but transmits the order to the destroyer screen. Cony and Beale receive it by early afternoon and cease their runs.

Evening: without the explosions her sonar has logged for hours, B-59, running low on air and battery charge, surfaces at approximately 9:15 p.m. local. American destroyers, holding under the new instruction, observe from a standoff distance. No searchlights, no warning shots, no boarding attempt. The submarine ventilates, recharges, and remains on the surface under observation. McNamara's 9:52 p.m. report to the president: the immediate crisis at sea has eased; Savitsky did not interpret the reduced contact as an attack signal requiring a response.

But the wider machinery keeps moving on its own schedule. The Joint Chiefs, meeting separately, draft a formal memorandum — their second in two days — renewing the call for air strikes against Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312, and ask for authority to bring the first strike package to final readiness. LeMay tells colleagues the submarine incident is proof, not reassurance: the Soviets probed and got away with it once; next time might be different. He wants the record to show delay is dangerous.

Robert Kennedy, separately, reopens his channel to Anatoly Dobrynin at the Soviet embassy, signaling Washington wants a fast, verifiable withdrawal arrangement and can offer a public non-invasion pledge. He does not commit the U.S. on Turkey; he asks whether it can be kept out of the public exchange and handled privately. Dobrynin's reply, and whether it goes back to Moscow before Khrushchev finalizes his own terms, is not yet known in Washington.

In Moscow, word reaches Khrushchev that B-59 surfaced without being fired on. He orders his Washington channel kept open and begins preparing to offer removal of the missiles for a non-invasion pledge, publicly, while holding the Turkish missile question in reserve for a private track. No cable has yet been received in Washington stating this in Moscow's own words; it is inferred from the pattern of Soviet signals, not confirmed by direct communication.

The president has ordered nothing about the Chiefs' launch-readiness request, nothing about which of Khrushchev's terms to answer or through what channel, and nothing further about Turkey. All three sit before him as decisions still to be made.
response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct, 1:40 p.m.–9:52 p.m.: Kennedy ordered the quarantine held and harassment of the submerged Soviet submarine stopped. The Chiefs objected but complied. That night B-59 surfaced without being fired on; the naval crisis eased. The Joint Chiefs formally renewed their demand for air strikes on Cuban SAM sites and requested launch-readiness authority — unanswered. RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel on a non-invasion pledge and a possible private deal on Turkey — unauthorized. Khrushchev, informed the submarine was spared, kept his channel open and moved to prepare public withdrawal terms while reserving Turkey privately.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, early afternoon. A U-2 was shot down and its pilot killed this morning; the quarantine holds; strategic forces stand at highest alert with no direct Washington-Moscow line. Kennedy ordered destroyers to hold quarantine stations but stop depth-charging a submerged Soviet submarine (B-59). The Chiefs objected on the record but complied. That night B-59 surfaced to recharge without being fired on; American destroyers observed but did not act. McNamara reports the immediate naval crisis eased, though missiles and Cuban air defenses remain operational. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs formally renewed their demand for air strikes against Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312) and requested final launch-readiness authority — unanswered. RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel, signaling a non-invasion pledge is possible and probing a private deal on Turkish missiles — no authority yet given on Turkey. Khrushchev, informed the submarine was not attacked, kept his Washington channel open and is preparing public terms (missile withdrawal for non-invasion pledge) while reserving Turkey privately. Kennedy has not yet decided which terms to answer, through what channel, or how to answer the Chiefs' strike request.

outcomes.event: Lyndon B. Johnson receives Kennedy's private demand and refuses to resign, telling the president that a vice president cannot be dismissed and that he will not abandon the administration during the Cuba crisis. When Kennedy's public request follows, Johnson issues a short statement that he remains vice president and is attending to his constitutional duties.
outcomes.because: In 1962 the president has no power to remove a vice president, and Johnson has powerful political reasons not to accept a humiliating, crisis-time expulsion.

response.title: A Vacancy That Does Not Exist
response.immediate: At 12:40 pm Kennedy, through Kenny O'Donnell, transmits a private request to Vice President Johnson that he resign the office effective immediately, citing the need to appoint Robert F. Kennedy. Johnson receives the message at the Executive Office Building and refuses within the hour, telling O'Donnell there is no vacancy for the president to fill and that he will not leave his post while Soviet missiles sit ninety miles from Florida. Kennedy's subsequent public statement, read to reporters at 2:15 pm, asks Johnson to step aside; Johnson's own one-paragraph statement, issued twenty minutes later, says he remains vice president and is attending to his constitutional duties.
response.worldReaction: Wire services carry both statements within the hour. No foreign government has yet commented; Moscow's press has not mentioned it as of 4:00 pm. Domestically, the split is now a matter of public record, running alongside the U-2 pilot's death and the quarantine on every afternoon broadcast.
response.consequences: Johnson remains vice president; no mechanism existed to remove him and none was used. General LeMay tells the Joint Chiefs the public rupture 'looks like paralysis' and presses again for authority against the SAM sites. McNamara continues to hold OPLAN 312 in readiness. Robert Kennedy keeps the Dobrynin channel open, signaling flexibility on withdrawal while withholding commitment on Turkey. The presidency now visibly disagrees with itself while every other mechanism of the crisis continues unaltered.
response.detailed: The message went by hand at 12:40 pm — O'Donnell to Johnson's military aide, then to Johnson directly in his EOB office, where he was reviewing quarantine dispositions with Vance. Johnson's reply, delivered orally and then in writing at 1:35 pm, was two sentences: the vice presidency is not an office a president can vacate by request, and he intends to remain at his post 'so long as Cuba is unresolved.' Kennedy's public statement followed at 2:15 pm in the West Wing pressroom, Pierre Salinger reading it to a dozen reporters already camped for Cuba briefings. Johnson's counter-statement at 2:35 pm, issued from his own press office without clearing language with the White House, was the first instance since January 1961 of the vice president publicly contradicting the president on a personal matter. In the Cabinet Room at 3:00 pm, McNamara asked flatly how many minutes this had cost the crisis management effort; no one answered him. LeMay, present for the 3:30 pm JCS briefing, told Kennedy the quarantine force and the strike squadrons need clear civilian leadership, 'not a family argument broadcast on three networks.' RFK, arriving from a second meeting with Dobrynin at 3:50 pm, reported the Soviet ambassador had not raised the Johnson matter, focused instead on withdrawal terms. The submarine incident near the quarantine line, the Jupiter question, and the SAM sites remain exactly where they stood at noon — untouched by this order, waiting on separate decisions.

press.headline: KENNEDY ASKS JOHNSON TO RESIGN VICE PRESIDENCY
press.body: President Kennedy this afternoon publicly requested that Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson resign, saying he wishes to appoint his brother, Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, to the office. No constitutional procedure exists for such a substitution absent Mr. Johnson's consent.

press.headline: JOHNSON: 'I REMAIN VICE PRESIDENT'
press.body: Vice President Johnson issued a statement twenty minutes after the President's remarks stating he has no intention of resigning and is 'attending to constitutional duties' amid the Cuban crisis. The statement did not address the President's stated reasons.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: How many minutes did this cost us, Mr. President? The Joint Chiefs are building an execution timetable on the SAM sites and now they have a headline about paralysis to wave at you. I'd like every hour from here forward spent on Dobrynin, not on the Vice President.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: With respect, Mr. President — the country just watched its own government split in public with a dead pilot in Cuba and Soviet missiles still armed. Give me authority on those SAM sites before the next U-2 goes down too.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin didn't even mention it — he's still talking withdrawal terms. But Lyndon's statement is going to run next to the quarantine story all night. Whatever we do next has to look like this administration still has one voice on Cuba.

response.chronicleEntry: At 12:40 pm on 27 October, President Kennedy privately requested Vice President Johnson's resignation to make way for Robert F. Kennedy; Johnson refused within the hour. Kennedy's 2:15 pm public request was met by Johnson's own public refusal at 2:35 pm — the first public presidential-vice presidential rupture of the administration. No vacancy was created. The missile crisis proceeded on all other tracks unchanged: the Dobrynin channel remained open, OPLAN 312 remained in readiness, and the Joint Chiefs pressed for strike authority against the SAM sites.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the Cuban Missile Crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing its pilot — the first combat death of the crisis. Soviet missiles remain on the island under a U.S. naval quarantine; strategic forces on both sides are at maximum alert; there is no hotline to Moscow. At noon, President Kennedy asked Vice President Johnson to resign, publicly and privately, intending to install Robert F. Kennedy. Johnson refused both times, issuing his own public statement that he remains vice president — an unprecedented public rupture now on the wire services alongside the crisis itself. Meanwhile RFK keeps a backchannel to Ambassador Dobrynin open, signaling flexibility on withdrawal without committing on the Turkish Jupiters; McNamara holds OPLAN 312 in readiness while urging restraint; General LeMay presses for strike authority against the SAM sites, citing the public split as proof of paralysis. The quarantine line, the submarine incident, and Khrushchev's two letters remain unresolved and awaiting presidential decision.

outcomes.event: The written ultimatum reaches Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson, but Johnson refuses to resign. He has his office acknowledge receipt, telephones Robert Kennedy to demand the President withdraw the threat, and retains the original demand as evidence; no resignation is delivered within fifteen minutes.
outcomes.because: A vice president is independently elected and the President has no constitutional power to dismiss or compel his resignation. Johnson has strong reason to treat a coerced resignation as politically and legally void.

response.title: The Fifteen Minutes Expire
response.immediate: 12:00–12:04 p.m.: A courier carries the President's written demand to the Vice President's office in the Executive Office Building. Johnson reads it standing. His secretary logs receipt at 12:06. No resignation follows. At 12:11, Johnson telephones the Attorney General, not the President, and speaks for four minutes. At 12:15 the deadline lapses. Nothing further arrives from Johnson's office. The Secret Service reports no order exists, and no one, has moved to compel his physical presence.
response.worldReaction: Robert Kennedy comes to the Cabinet Room directly from the call, visibly shaken, and tells the President plainly that Johnson is not resigning and considers the demand to be kept as evidence. He warns that any attempt to force it further becomes public within hours. LeMay, waiting on the strike recommendation, treats the delay in the room as further proof that indecision has become policy. McNamara says only that he needs to know how many minutes remain before the SAM question forces itself.
response.consequences: No lawful mechanism exists to compel a vice president's resignation; none has been found in the past fifteen minutes and none is being sought now. Johnson's office has not disclosed the matter outside itself, so far as is known. The military track continues on its own schedule: OPLAN 312 sits ready, the Joint Chiefs' objection to further delay stands on the record, and the quarantine line remains active. The Dobrynin channel remains open but answered by no American terms yet.
response.detailed: By 12:15 the Cabinet Room holds the accumulated weight of two unresolved crises where there had been one. The pilot's death this morning, the SAM sites, LeMay's package sitting cocked — all of it now sits alongside a vice president who has been ordered to resign and has simply declined, in writing acknowledgment only, through a secretary's hand and a lawyer's silence. Robert Kennedy did not raise his voice on the phone with Johnson; he does not raise it now. He says: this cannot be forced, there's no statute, there's no procedure, and if you try to march Secret Service into his office you will hand Khrushchev the finest photograph of the decade. LeMay, standing by the window with a marked map of Cuban SAM installations, says the Cabinet Room has spent fifteen minutes finding out that an order can be given and refused; he asks whether authorization for the strike package will suffer the same fate. McNamara does not look up from his notepad; he asks only whether the Navy's rules of engagement at the quarantine line have changed while this occurred; the answer is that they have not, on his order, and will not without further instruction. The clock reads 12:19. Johnson's office is quiet. Dobrynin has said nothing new since morning. The pilot's body is being catalogued in Florida. The teletype in the next room continues to print unrelated traffic, three minutes old.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, he's not resigning, and I told him you'd say that in the heat of the morning — I did not tell him it was withdrawn, because you haven't withdrawn it. He's keeping the paper. If this gets out before Cuba is settled, we lose the country regardless of how Cuba ends.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Fifteen minutes to find out an order doesn't work is fifteen minutes the SAM sites didn't get hit. I've got crews sitting in cockpits since 0900. At some point 'unresolved' becomes the policy, Mr. President, and it's not one the Joint Chiefs signed onto.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: I'd like a number, not a mood. How many minutes before the Johnson matter forces a public statement — one, or six? I can plan around a number. The quarantine line hasn't moved. I'd like to know if that's still your intention before I'm asked something I can't answer for Admiral Anderson.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–12:19 EST, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy issued Vice President Johnson a written ultimatum demanding immediate resignation within fifteen minutes, with force to compel his presence at the White House threatened if he refused. Johnson's office acknowledged receipt at 12:06 but delivered no resignation. Johnson telephoned Attorney General Robert Kennedy at 12:11, refused to comply, and retained the demand. No lawful mechanism to compel resignation was identified, and no order to physically bring Johnson to the White House was issued. The fifteen-minute deadline lapsed at 12:15 unresolved. Meanwhile, OPLAN 312 strike package remained on hold per McNamara pending the Dobrynin channel; the Joint Chiefs formally recorded objection to further delay; the quarantine line held station without incident.
response.storySoFar: Noon, 27 October 1962: a U-2 pilot is dead over Cuba, Soviet MRBMs remain emplaced, the quarantine holds, no hotline exists. Robert Kennedy runs a private channel to Ambassador Dobrynin probing a non-invasion-for-removal trade against Khrushchev's harder public terms. The Joint Chiefs and LeMay press for an immediate strike on the SAM sites via OPLAN 312; McNamara holds it ready but unlaunched, protecting the diplomatic channel. At noon the President demanded Vice President Johnson resign in writing within fifteen minutes, threatening forcible transport to the White House. Johnson refused, kept the letter as evidence, and called Robert Kennedy rather than complying. No lawful means to compel him exists and none was found. The deadline expired at 12:15 with Johnson still in office, the matter undisclosed outside his staff so far as known, and the missile crisis's military and diplomatic tracks both still open and unresolved beneath a now-compounding constitutional crisis of the President's own making.

assumesUnmet: A suitable aircraft and crew have not yet been confirmed.

outcomes.event: LeMay orders the first U-2 SAC can put forward to proceed without waiting for a fresh availability and route-safety review. The aircraft crosses Cuba, is tracked by Soviet and Cuban radar, and is hit by an SA-2 before its film can be recovered; Kennedy receives word that a second American reconnaissance crew is missing or dead, while Washington still lacks the photographs the sortie was meant to obtain.
outcomes.because: Proceeding immediately treats the unconfirmed aircraft-and-crew prerequisite as an administrative detail, but the Cuban air-defence network has already demonstrated that an unescorted high-altitude U-2 can be engaged.

establishes.statement: A second U.S. reconnaissance aircraft has been lost over Cuba or is missing after entering Cuban airspace, and its intelligence product is unavailable to Washington.
Soviet and Cuban air-defence commanders know that the United States has resumed overflight reconnaissance after Anderson's death.

opensThreads.title: A Second Shootdown
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy retaliate against the SA-2 network, or maintain the quarantine and diplomatic track after another loss?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A decision on OPLAN 312 or an explicit decision not to retaliate.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: LeMay and the Joint Chiefs cite the unavenged loss as grounds for immediate air strikes.

createsUnknowns.statement: The fate of the assigned U-2 pilot after the aircraft's loss is unconfirmed.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether the pilot survived, was captured, or was killed.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Cuban or Soviet public reporting, intercepted communications, or a later repatriation.

assumesMet: The president's authority to direct reconnaissance is established.
assumesUnmet: No confirmed aircraft, crew, route, or current threat assessment was obtained before launch.

outcomes.event: Robert McNamara requires the Joint Chiefs to confirm a serviceable aircraft, a rested crew, weather, route, recovery plan, and coordination with the Navy before releasing the single sortie. LeMay protests that this has turned a simple allocation order into a new reconnaissance planning operation; the review consumes the turn, but SAC and Navy commands produce a named mission package rather than launching blind.
outcomes.because: The missing prerequisite can be covered only by asking the military to identify and certify an actual asset and crew, which necessarily adds planning, interservice coordination, and a safety review beyond Kennedy's narrow directive.

establishes.statement: The reconnaissance directive has expanded into a cross-service mission-planning and availability-confirmation process rather than an immediate allocation.
No reconnaissance sortie has launched during this turn because the military is assembling the additional mission package.

opensThreads.title: Mission Package Beyond the Order
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy approve the broader, safer reconnaissance package, including the route and any Navy support it requires?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Presidential approval, a demand for a narrower mission, or cancellation.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The added planning delays intelligence while the Chiefs renew their case that only OPLAN 312 can suppress the SAM threat.

assumesMet: The president's authority to issue the original reconnaissance directive is established.
assumesUnmet: A suitable aircraft and crew were not already confirmed; covering that gap required an operational step outside the stated mandate.

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs allocate a Navy low-level photographic sortie instead of another U-2, judging it the only reconnaissance asset they can promptly assign with a crew and recovery plan. The aircraft returns with usable imagery of missile-site activity, but Cuban troops fire on it during its run; Fidel Castro is told that American aircraft are now making low passes over Cuban territory and orders his forces to treat further overflights as invasion preparation.
outcomes.because: A low-level naval mission can be organized more quickly than a fresh high-altitude U-2 mission, but it is conspicuous, directly menaces Cuban ground forces, and gives Castro evidence for his expectation of an imminent attack.

establishes.statement: The United States has obtained new reconnaissance imagery from Cuba through a Navy low-level photographic sortie.
Cuban military and political leadership know that U.S. reconnaissance flights are continuing at low altitude and are preparing to fire on subsequent intrusions.

opensThreads.title: Images and Interpretation
opensThreads.question: What do the recovered photographs prove about the operational state of the Soviet missiles, and will Washington act on them before diplomacy can close?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A completed intelligence assessment followed by a presidential decision.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs and civilian advisers will draw competing conclusions from partial imagery.

opensThreads.title: Castro's Air-Defence Order
opensThreads.question: Will Cuban forces fire on the next American overflight without Soviet authorization?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A subsequent overflight, a Soviet restraint order, or a halt to U.S. reconnaissance.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Local Cuban commanders remain on heightened expectation of attack.

createsUnknowns.statement: The low-level photographs have reached Washington but have not yet been fully interpreted.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether the images show missiles ready for launch, continued construction, or evidence relevant to a negotiated withdrawal.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: The CIA and military photographic-intelligence readout.

assumesMet: The president's authority to order reconnaissance is established.
Military commands identify a Navy photographic asset and crew able to fly promptly.

outcomes.event: LeMay accepts the reconnaissance order but records a formal objection that no further aircraft should be sent over Cuba unless Kennedy simultaneously authorizes OPLAN 312 against the SA-2 sites. He tells the Executive Committee that he will execute the single-sortie order, while the Joint Chiefs' written recommendation for strikes reaches the president alongside it, making the civilian-military split impossible to keep private for long.
outcomes.because: After Anderson's death, the Chiefs regard reconnaissance without suppression of Cuban air defences as exposing another crew for little gain; they cannot lawfully refuse the order, but can force their dissent onto the record.

establishes.statement: LeMay and the Joint Chiefs have formally linked their compliance with the reconnaissance directive to a renewed recommendation for OPLAN 312 air strikes.
The disagreement between Kennedy and his senior military leadership now exists in a written operational record.

opensThreads.title: The Chiefs' Written Dissent
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy authorize OPLAN 312, overrule the Chiefs in writing, or replace commanders who make the reconnaissance mission conditional in practice?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential strike decision or a clear command decision on the Chiefs' objection.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The dissent is increasingly likely to leak, damaging command control and narrowing Kennedy's room to negotiate.

assumesMet: The president's authority to issue a lawful reconnaissance order is established.
assumesUnmet: The identity and readiness of a specific reconnaissance aircraft and crew remain unconfirmed.

strategy_compiler:Interpretation:d96629e.request:
You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: results that depend on another party choosing to comply
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs transmit Kennedy’s restriction through the Navy chain: the destroyers maintain the quarantine screen but stop dropping practice depth charges and break off close harassment of B-59. After hours of silence, Captain Valentin Savitsky brings the exhausted submarine to the surface; U.S. ships observe it withdraw without firing.

A direct presidential restraint order can be executed by the armed forces despite the Joint Chiefs’ preference for escalation.

opensThreads.question: Will B-59 return toward the Soviet Union, attempt to re-enter the quarantine area, or report that it was attacked?

outcomes.event: The Navy obeys Kennedy’s order, but too late to undo the fear created aboard B-59. Believing the depth charges marked the opening of war, Captain Valentin Savitsky and political officer Ivan Maslennikov vote to fire the nuclear torpedo; Vasili Arkhipov fails to prevent release. The detonation destroys a U.S. destroyer near the quarantine line, killing its crew and making a Soviet nuclear attack on American forces an observed fact before Washington can clarify the order.
outcomes.because: Kennedy can halt American pressure but cannot command officers cut off from Moscow, already exhausted, overheated, and convinced that hostilities may have begun.

establishes.statement: A nuclear weapon has detonated against U.S. naval forces at the quarantine line, destroying a U.S. destroyer and killing its crew.

findings.claim: The player’s order only instructs the Joint Chiefs to hold the quarantine line and avoid escalatory contact; nothing in the directive mentions a parallel diplomatic channel. Outcome_3 invents an entirely new mechanism—Robert Kennedy approaching Dobrynin and asking Moscow to order the submarine to surface—that the player never specified, effectively supplying coordination and initiative beyond the scope of the military order.

The prerequisites explicitly flag that the Joint Chiefs might resist, resign, or refuse the order as reckless, calling this 'ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE.' Yet no outcome models outright non-compliance or delayed/half-hearted execution by the Chiefs (as opposed to compliance-with-protest in outcome_4). A scenario where the order is slow-walked or partially disregarded, allowing continued harassment despite the president's directive, is a plausible outcome the enumeration omits.

Outcome_2 depicts a Soviet nuclear torpedo destroying a U.S. destroyer near the quarantine line as an isolated, contained event that Washington might still 'clarify' afterward. Given the stakes described elsewhere (risk of irreversible escalation toward nuclear exchange), a nuclear detonation against a U.S. warship would almost certainly trigger immediate full-scale retaliation or crisis escalation rather than remain a localized incident awaiting clarification.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: 1600 hours EDT. The Navy chain confirms Kennedy's restriction transmitted: destroyers cease depth-charge harassment and close signalling against B-59. For nearly three hours the line holds without contact. At approximately 1855, lookouts on USS Cony report the submarine surfacing roughly eight miles inside the quarantine zone. No weapon is fired. B-59 withdraws to the east on the surface, running lights visible, diesel engines audible over open radio traffic monitored by SIGINT.
response.worldReaction: Moscow says nothing officially about the encounter. Dobrynin, through Robert Kennedy's channel, signals only that Khrushchev's terms of two days prior — missile withdrawal for a non-invasion pledge — remain the basis for discussion, and asks Washington to avoid further incidents while the exchange continues. Havana radio continues its call to resistance. The Joint Chiefs, informed the submarine withdrew without incident, treat this as confirmation that pressure works — and press harder for OPLAN 312.
response.consequences: LeMay's renewed strike recommendation sits on the table unresolved. McNamara has ordered strike plans prepared but not executed, preserving the quarantine and surveillance in the meantime. RFK's message to Dobrynin has gone out but Moscow's answer on verification and the harder Turkish-missile terms remains unheard. The president must now decide whether to answer Khrushchev's easier terms, what assurance to offer, and whether restraint continues to hold against his own chiefs.
response.detailed:
The Cabinet Room at 1900: overhead lights against the dark windows, coffee gone cold on the table, McNamara standing at the map board with a pointer resting on the quarantine line south of Bermuda. He reports the sequence flatly — order transmitted 1620, harassment ceased by 1640, no further sonar contact logged until the surfacing at 1855. 'Eight miles inside the line, Mr. President. They came up on their own. Nobody fired on them and they didn't fire on us.' He wants that understood as the mechanism working, not luck.

LeMay is on his feet before McNamara finishes. He calls the surfacing an accident of Soviet fatigue, not a settlement, and returns to the SAM sites: every hour without a strike is an hour Moscow uses to disperse warheads or harden positions. He wants OPLAN 312 authorized tonight, while daylight photography from the morning's runs is still current.

Robert Kennedy, by the telephone alcove, has just come off the line with Dobrynin. He tells his brother the ambassador took the message on prevention of further incidents without commitment, and repeated that Khrushchev's public position — missiles out for a no-invasion pledge — still stands as the offer to work from, separate from the harder demand about Turkey raised in the second, unpublished letter. RFK's read: answer the easier terms now, before Saturday closes, and leave the harder terms unaddressed rather than reject them outright.

The Joint Chiefs' written submission is on the table: quarantine restriction acknowledged and complied with, but strike authorization requested again, citing continued exposure of U.S. surveillance aircraft and the destroyer screen to further incidents like the one just concluded. No decision has been made on it.

Outside, the quarantine line holds unchanged. Havana's exhortations continue over shortwave. Nothing has come back from Moscow beyond what Dobrynin said in the RFK channel. The room waits on what the president answers, and on what — if anything — arrives from the Kremlin overnight.

press.headline: SOVIET SUBMARINE SURFACES, WITHDRAWS FROM QUARANTINE ZONE — NO SHOTS FIRED, NAVY SAYS
press.body: A Pentagon spokesman confirmed this evening that a Soviet submarine, tracked for several hours within the naval quarantine zone, surfaced and withdrew without incident. The spokesman declined to characterize the vessel's earlier movements or to say whether U.S. forces had made contact with it.

press.headline: IMPERIALIST PROVOCATIONS CONTINUE DESPITE HEROIC SOVIET RESTRAINT
press.body: Cuban commentators denounced the continued U.S. naval blockade as an act of war and called for full readiness among Cuban militia units, stating that any further incident at sea would be laid at Washington's door.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Three hours, no contact, no weapon fired. That is the order working as intended, Mr. President — the alternative sequence, if we'd kept up the harassment, I can walk you through it, and it does not end here. I'd hold this posture and let the Dobrynin channel run before anyone in this room decides otherwise.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: That submarine surfaced because it was out of air, not because we were gentle with it. It tells us nothing about the SAM sites, which are still there, still tracking our aircraft. We have daylight photography from this morning. I want authorization tonight, before it goes stale.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin didn't reject anything — he didn't commit to anything either, which from him is close to agreement. Answer the missiles-for-non-invasion offer now, tonight if you can, and don't let Bobby's second letter or Curtis's sites become the reason we lose the hour we've got.

response.chronicleEntry: 1855 EDT, 27 October: Soviet submarine B-59 surfaced inside the quarantine line and withdrew without weapons fired, after Kennedy's order halted U.S. depth-charge harassment. Joint Chiefs complied but renewed their recommendation for strikes on Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312), still unauthorized. RFK-Dobrynin channel held open on missiles-for-non-invasion terms; Moscow's formal answer not yet received.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba this morning. Kennedy ordered the quarantine held but restrained U.S. destroyers from further harassment of the submerged Soviet submarine B-59. The order was transmitted and obeyed through the Navy chain; after hours of silence, B-59 surfaced near 1855 EDT and withdrew without incident. The Joint Chiefs complied with the restriction but renewed pressure for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites, which Kennedy has not authorized. McNamara has prepared strike plans without executing them. Robert Kennedy, via the Dobrynin backchannel, kept open Khrushchev's public terms — missile withdrawal for a U.S. non-invasion pledge — while asking Moscow to prevent further incidents; Moscow's formal reply is not yet in hand, and the harder, second-letter demand regarding Turkey remains unaddressed. Havana continues to call for resistance. No nuclear or conventional weapon has been fired by either side. The quarantine line remains in force, unchanged, as evening falls on Washington.

response.title: One Sortie, No Aircraft
response.immediate: At 12:04 p.m. Kennedy directed the Joint Chiefs to allocate a single reconnaissance sortie over the missile sites. The order passed to General Curtis LeMay at Strategic Air Command, who logged compliance and began assigning aircraft and crew. By 4:00 p.m., four hours into the window, no U-2 had left the ground; SAC named neither pilot nor tail number in the reporting reaching the Cabinet Room.
response.worldReaction: The Joint Chiefs reported the order accepted and in preparation, satisfying the formal requirement without producing a flight. LeMay used the same hours to fix a route over the missile area and to keep OPLAN 312 postured for execution. The Chiefs separately submitted a follow-on strike contingency tied to any further aircraft loss — submitted alongside, not in place of, the reconnaissance compliance.
response.consequences: McNamara tightened control procedures over reconnaissance and quarantine operations and warned against any strike preceding a further diplomatic move. Robert Kennedy used the Dobrynin channel to press for verifiable withdrawal while opening discussion of a non-invasion assurance. Cuban air defenses remained on heightened alert. The sortie itself — aircraft, pilot, launch time — stayed unresolved at day's end.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room at 12:15: Kennedy at the head of the table, McNamara standing near the map easel with the morning's Jack Anderson photographs, cigarette smoke thick over the coffee service. The president's order was simple — one sortie, next available window — and by the routine of things should have produced a launch within hours. It did not. General LeMay took the order at SAC headquarters in Omaha and, by the accounts reaching Washington, assigned an aircraft and a crew and drew a route over the missile sites, but named neither publicly nor in the compliance cable that reached the Chiefs by 3:00 p.m. The Joint Chiefs reported the order accepted; that report was itself the only concrete deliverable of the four hours. Whether SAC's internal readiness meant a genuine near-term launch, or meant LeMay folding the sortie into his broader pressure to keep OPLAN 312 primed, could not be told from Washington. McNamara, working the telephone to CINCLANT and reading loss-rate tables, ordered tighter control of reconnaissance timing and quarantine intercepts, telling the president flatly that a strike undertaken before Moscow had answered the private channel would be a decision with no recall. Robert Kennedy, using the number he had used before, told Dobrynin at the Soviet Embassy that Washington needed verified removal, not a promise, and that assurances against invasion could be discussed privately once removal was underway — and asked, in turn, what Moscow's own terms were. No answer had come back by 4:00 p.m. The Chiefs, for their part, treated LeMay's readiness posture as prudent and used the four hours to draft a contingency strike plan keyed to any further loss of an American aircraft, submitting it alongside their report of compliance rather than instead of it. At day's end: the reconnaissance order stood accepted, unexecuted, and unaccounted for in specifics; the SAM and strike plans stood ready; the Dobrynin channel stood open, unanswered.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "Compliance isn't the same as an aircraft in the air, Mr. President. I want the tail number and the launch time before I call this resolved. Until I have both, I'm treating the sortie as pending, not done.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "The mission is assigned. SAC does not sit on its hands, and neither should the Chiefs sit on OPLAN 312. Every hour we hold that plan on the shelf instead of the runway is an hour we hand the Soviets to finish hardening those sites.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Dobrynin took it seriously — I could hear that much. But he didn't give me terms, Jack, he gave me silence with good manners. We need Khrushchev's own words, not his ambassador's patience.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–16:00, 27 October. Kennedy ordered one reconnaissance sortie allocated. Joint Chiefs reported compliance; LeMay assigned aircraft, crew, and route at SAC but no launch occurred by 16:00. Chiefs separately submitted a contingency strike plan tied to further aircraft loss. McNamara tightened reconnaissance and quarantine controls, warning against preemptive strike. RFK opened Dobrynin channel on verifiable withdrawal and non-invasion terms; no Soviet reply received.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot killed — first combat death of the crisis. Kennedy, seeking verified missile removal without nuclear war, ordered one further reconnaissance sortie at noon. SAC's LeMay logged compliance and assigned an aircraft and route but none launched within four hours; the Joint Chiefs simultaneously drafted a contingency strike plan for any further U.S. loss and kept OPLAN 312 primed. McNamara tightened control over reconnaissance and quarantine operations, warning strongly against striking before diplomacy had a chance. Robert Kennedy opened the Dobrynin channel, offering discussion of non-invasion assurances tied to verified withdrawal, and asked for Moscow's terms — none received yet. No hotline exists; all Soviet responses arrive with delay. Quarantine remains in force, Cuban defenses on heightened alert, both sides at unprecedented strategic readiness. The reconnaissance sortie ordered this turn remains unexecuted and unaccounted for in specifics.

readings.reasoning: The private Kennedy–Khrushchev channel and Khrushchev's willingness to negotiate reduce immediate escalation, but Cuban maximum alert, active U.S. strike preparations, and continued Joint Chiefs pressure keep tension extremely high.

The emerging U.S.–Soviet negotiating framework modestly improves coordination around an exit, while Castro's opposition and the Joint Chiefs' insistence on a strike expose serious divisions within the opposing camps.
The events produce no clear public shift because the Kennedy–Dobrynin contact remains secret, though continued military readiness preserves political support for a firm stance.

Presidential control is strained by LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressing for immediate action, Castro directing Cuban forces independently, and multiple forces remaining at high readiness despite McNamara's effort to preserve a controlled delay.

The oral assurance, Dobrynin's successful cable to Moscow, and Khrushchev's proposed missile-withdrawal and non-invasion deal substantially expand room for a negotiated settlement, despite the unresolved Turkish demand and Castro's resistance.

response.title: The Backchannel Holds
response.immediate: At 10:15 p.m., Robert Kennedy telephones the president from the Justice Department. Dobrynin took the assurance, said little, and left for the Soviet Embassy to cable Moscow. No text was exchanged, no signature — only the spoken word, as instructed. Robert reports Dobrynin's manner as grave but not hostile.
response.worldReaction: There is no public reaction, because there is no public event. Radio Moscow's 11 p.m. broadcast repeats Khrushchev's earlier withdrawal terms without amendment. TASS is silent on any private contact. In Washington, the Cabinet Room empties toward midnight with Robert McNamara still at the map table, reconnaissance officers cycling in with fresh U-2 and low-level Crusader film from Saturday's overflights.
response.consequences: OPLAN 312 strike packages remain cocked at Homestead and Key West on McNamara's order — readiness maintained, execution withheld. The Joint Chiefs, through General Taylor, renew their written recommendation for a strike on the SAM sites within twenty-four hours if no verified withdrawal begins. LeMay tells the Joint Staff privately that the channel is "buying Castro's engineers another sunrise." Nothing from Moscow arrives before this session closes.
response.detailed:
Robert Kennedy's meeting with Dobrynin took place in the Attorney General's office at the Justice Department shortly after nine that evening, unscheduled, no note-takers. He delivered the assurance as the president framed it — orally, deniable, non-binding on paper. Dobrynin listened, asked clarifying questions about sequencing, and made no commitment beyond agreeing to transmit the substance to Moscow that night on a cable Robert believes went out within the hour, given Soviet Embassy traffic patterns during the crisis. There is no receipt for this. There is no way, from the Cabinet Room, to know whether the cable reached Khrushchev before or after his own reply is drafted, whether Malinovsky or the Presidium sees it first, or whether it travels intact. The assurance itself remains unacknowledged by any Soviet organ of state as of midnight.

Meanwhile the machinery underneath continues on the orders already given this morning: DEFCON 2 for Strategic Air Command, quarantine picket ships holding stations along the barrier line, low-level reconnaissance sorties scheduled to resume at first light over the MRBM sites at San Cristóbal and Sagua la Grande. The Joint Chiefs' recommendation for an immediate strike on the SAM installations — the same batteries that killed Major Rudolf Anderson that morning — sits on McNamara's desk, endorsed unanimously, awaiting presidential response. McNamara argues for a defined window; Taylor and LeMay want language that expires. The submarine that surfaced near the quarantine line earlier in the day has not yet been given fresh rules of engagement for this watch; that order remains outstanding.

No public statement has been made about the Dobrynin channel. Congress has not been briefed. The public record, as of this session's close, still shows only the quarantine, the shootdown, and Khrushchev's public terms from the radio broadcast — nothing of what passed in the Attorney General's office an hour before midnight.

press.headline: NO WORD FROM WHITE HOUSE ON U-2 LOSS RESPONSE
press.body: Officials at the White House late Saturday declined to say whether the United States would retaliate for the loss of the reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba, or how it intended to respond to Premier Khrushchev's broadcast terms. A spokesman said only that 'the President is reviewing the situation with his advisors.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin took it. He didn't blink, he didn't argue, he just listened and wrote nothing down — that's what I wanted. But I want you to know he asked twice about timing, which tells me Moscow is worried about how fast this has to move. We should have an answer ready to send the moment anything comes back, because Curtis and Max Taylor aren't going to sit quiet past tomorrow noon.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: We have no confirmation of transmission, no confirmation of receipt, and no timeline for a Soviet response. I count that as an unknown, not a result. I've held the strike packages at readiness without launch authority — that buys us perhaps eighteen to twenty-four hours before the Chiefs' recommendation becomes, in effect, the only plan on the table by default of nothing else moving.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, while we're waiting on a Soviet ambassador to walk across town, the crews at those SAM sites are getting a second night to disperse or dig in. We had a pilot killed this morning. The recommendation from the Chiefs stands unanimous. Every hour this channel doesn't produce something in writing is an hour we're not doing what we already agreed we might have to do.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, ~2100–midnight EST: RFK delivers oral assurance to Dobrynin at Justice Dept per presidential instruction; Dobrynin transmits substance to Moscow via cable, timing and content of transmission unconfirmed. No Soviet acknowledgment received by midnight. Strike packages (OPLAN 312) held at readiness on McNamara's order; JCS renew unanimous strike recommendation. Quarantine and DEFCON 2 posture unchanged. No public or congressional disclosure of the Dobrynin channel.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing Major Anderson — the crisis's first combat death. Khrushchev broadcast public terms: missile withdrawal for a U.S. non-invasion pledge, with an unresolved Turkish-missile demand. Kennedy ordered Robert Kennedy to deliver a private oral assurance to Ambassador Dobrynin through the backchannel; Dobrynin accepted it without commitment and cabled Moscow, with no confirmed receipt or Soviet response yet. OPLAN 312 airstrikes against Cuban SAM sites remain prepared but withheld; McNamara counsels a bounded diplomatic window while the Joint Chiefs, backed by LeMay, press unanimously for immediate strike authority. DEFCON 2 and the naval quarantine remain in force. A Soviet submarine surfaced near the quarantine line with rules of engagement for the next watch still unset. No public or congressional disclosure of the private channel has been made.

The assassination operation’s exposure and competing pressure for immediate strikes versus controlled quarantine create additional strain among Washington’s civilian and military leadership and partners.

McNamara’s requirement for explicit attack authority is directly challenged by renewed Joint Chiefs recommendations and LeMay’s private pressure to proceed, exposing serious civil-military control friction.

response.title: The Courier Taken
response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. John McCone telephoned Richard Helms from his office at CIA headquarters and passed the President's instruction: activate the exile and Havana-based assets against Fidel Castro, target within seven days. Helms had no live channel to Castro's person. An exile courier carrying the operational cable was stopped and taken by Cuban State Security before he reached his contact in Havana. No attempt on Castro occurred. Separately, the order for the armed forces to muster all resources produced no new deployment; Robert McNamara held the existing strike package at readiness and imposed a requirement for explicit presidential authority before any attack proceeds.
response.worldReaction: Havana has said nothing publicly. Whether Cuban interrogators have connected the seized courier to Washington, or to the President by name, is not known from any source available to this room. Moscow has given no indication it is aware of the attempt. Dobrynin, contacted separately by Robert Kennedy, discussed only non-invasion assurances and verified missile withdrawal — the Castro operation did not enter that exchange.
response.consequences: The Joint Chiefs renewed their recommendation for immediate strikes on the SAM sites, citing Anderson's death that morning. LeMay is telling other officers privately that further delay is surrender by installment. McNamara's tightened rules of engagement now sit directly against that pressure. The compromised Castro operation remains neither terminated nor contained — Cuban security holds a captured cable and a captured courier, and what either will yield is unknown.
response.detailed:
12:40 p.m., Cabinet Room. McCone left the table to place the call to Helms from an adjoining phone; the instruction he gave was terse — assets, one week, no further specification committed to paper in this room. Helms's existing Havana network had no confirmed route to Castro's person; the courier selected to carry instructions to an exile contact inside Cuba was intercepted by Cuban State Security before that contact was made. The operation has not reached its objective and has not been abandoned. Whether the courier has disclosed the cable's origin, or whether Cuban officers can trace it to Washington, is not established by anything received in this room as of 4:00 p.m.

The order to muster the full armed forces met the machinery already in place: DEFCON readiness, the quarantine line, the strike package assembled since the missile sites were first photographed. McNamara did not expand it; he tightened control, directing that no attack begin at the quarantine line or elsewhere without his or the President's explicit word. The Joint Chiefs, unmoved by that instruction, placed before the President again their recommendation for immediate strikes on the SAM sites, arguing every additional hour raises the chance the missiles become operational. LeMay pressed privately for OPLAN 312 to proceed regardless of the diplomatic track Robert Kennedy is running through Dobrynin — a channel that, this afternoon, addressed only non-invasion and verified withdrawal, saying nothing of Turkey and nothing of Castro.

No strike has been ordered. No word has come from Moscow on any subject raised since noon. The courier remains in Cuban hands.

press.headline: MILITARY CHIEFS URGE ACTION AFTER U-2 LOSS, ADMINISTRATION SOURCES SAY DEBATE CONTINUES
press.body: Sources close to the Pentagon indicate senior military leadership has again pressed for direct action against Cuban air defenses following this morning's loss of a reconnaissance aircraft and its pilot. No White House statement has been issued on the substance of internal deliberations.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: I've held the package at readiness, Mr. President, but I want it clear — nothing fires without your word or mine passed forward in writing. As for the other matter, I'd like to know how many minutes separate 'seized' from 'talking,' because that's the number that determines what we're exposed to, and right now nobody can give it to me.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You had McCone chasing a courier through back streets in Havana while Anderson's widow gets a telegram. That's not a policy, that's a distraction. Give me the order on the SAM sites and I'll give you results you can measure by sundown.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, if that courier talks — and we have to assume he might — Castro hands Khrushchev a gift he didn't ask for and didn't need. I'm running Dobrynin on withdrawal and a pledge not to invade. If Moscow hears in the same week that we tried to kill Castro, that channel is worthless. You need to decide whether this operation is worth what it could cost us there.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October, 12:40–4:00 p.m. EST: On presidential instruction, McCone directed Helms to activate assets against Castro within one week; the courier carrying operational instructions was intercepted by Cuban State Security prior to contact. No attempt on Castro occurred. Order for full mustering of armed forces produced no expansion beyond existing readiness; McNamara imposed explicit-authority requirement for any attack. JCS renewed strike recommendation on SAM sites; LeMay pressed privately for OPLAN 312. RFK-Dobrynin channel addressed non-invasion and verified withdrawal only. Status of captured courier and cable unknown to Washington.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down that morning over Cuba, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Quarantine holds; Soviet missiles remain in Cuba; no hotline exists. At noon, President Kennedy ordered the CIA to assassinate Castro within a week and the armed forces to muster fully. McCone/Helms activated Havana assets, but the exile courier carrying instructions was seized by Cuban State Security before reaching Castro's circle — no attempt occurred, and whether Washington's hand has been exposed is unknown. Armed forces readiness was not expanded; McNamara instead tightened attack authority requirements even as the Joint Chiefs renewed demands for immediate SAM-site strikes and LeMay pushed privately for OPLAN 312. Robert Kennedy, via Dobrynin, opened discussion of non-invasion assurances and verified missile withdrawal, withholding any Turkish-missile commitment. No response has come from Moscow. The compromised Castro operation remains live and unresolved, a hidden liability inside an otherwise diplomatic opening.

outcomes.because: Kennedy can order the Air Force and crew to fly, but neither an unescorted presidential aircraft nor its radio calls can compel Havana to admit it. Castro, expecting an invasion, treats the approach as a possible prelude to attack rather than a diplomatic visit.

The Joint Chiefs’ written objections and LeMay’s publicized demand for a strike widened the gap between civilian diplomacy and military strategy, while Castro’s pressure on Moscow strained Soviet-Cuban alignment.

The humiliating interception and Castro’s apparent defiance likely weakened confidence in restraint, even as the administration’s avoidance of combat preserves some support for its handling of the crisis.

Cuban forces acted aggressively against the presidential aircraft while U.S. commanders pressed for an immediate strike despite civilian efforts to maintain contact without firing, exposing serious control frictions.

The Dobrynin channel and Kennedy’s proposed pause-and-verification exchange opened a possible off-ramp, but the public interception, Castro’s refusal of access, and competing demands over invasion and the quarantine narrowed it.

response.title: The Turnback
response.immediate: At 12:47 p.m. Air Force One (call sign Angel) departed Andrews without fighter escort, the President aboard, bound for Havana with no clearance from Cuban air defense. At 1:19 p.m., roughly forty miles south of Key West, two Cuban MiG-21s intercepted, forming up on the aircraft's wingtips. The pilot, on his own authority and against no contrary order reaching him in time, turned north. Air Force One landed back at Andrews at 2:38 p.m. Havana was never entered. No contact with Castro occurred.
response.worldReaction: By 3 p.m. Havana radio was broadcasting Castro's statement: the interception proved Washington intended invasion under cover of diplomacy, and Cuba's militia and coastal batteries were going to full readiness. General LeMay circulated a memo to the Chiefs by 3:30 p.m. demanding the SAM network be struck before dark, calling the turnback proof that delay itself was now the dangerous course. The Joint Chiefs delivered a written warning: a second incident involving American aircraft could produce escalation no one could control.
response.consequences: McNamara wants minutes, not opinions, and is waiting on radar logs from the interception before he will speak to risk. RFK is furious that the flight left Andrews without his brother telling him first, and is pressing to keep the incident out of the press pool report while the Dobrynin channel is still open. Nothing is known yet of how Moscow is reading the intercepted flight — as reconnaissance, as an aborted strike, or as something Castro is exaggerating past what the Kremlin believes.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room emptied within minutes of the order reaching Andrews Tower. By 12:50 p.m. Kenny O'Donnell was on the phone confirming the aircraft was airborne; nobody in the room had cleared it with Defense, State, or the Cuban government, because there had been no time and no channel to do so. McNamara arrived at 1:05 p.m., asked for the transponder track, and said nothing else until it was in his hand. At 1:19 p.m. NORAD relayed the MiG intercept; McNamara read the altitude and closure figures twice and said only, 'They had time to make a decision. They made the cautious one.' RFK, arriving at 1:40 p.m., asked first whether his brother was safe, second whether the press knew, and was told wire services already had it from a Key West ham operator's traffic. LeMay's memo came in at 3:30 p.m., blunt: the SAMs should be down by nightfall, and every hour since the intercept had made the world more dangerous, not less. The JCS written warning followed at 3:52 p.m., unsigned by McNamara, warning that a second aircraft incident — Cuban or American — could produce uncontrolled escalation. Castro's broadcast, monitored by CIA at 3:05 p.m., framed the flight as an unescorted incursion consistent with imminent invasion and called on Khrushchev not to trade Cuba's security for Soviet convenience. No word has come back from Moscow on how the Kremlin is reading any of it. The Dobrynin channel remains open but untested since this morning.

press.headline: PRESIDENTIAL AIRCRAFT TURNED BACK BY CUBAN JETS SOUTH OF FLORIDA
press.body: Unconfirmed reports from Key West describe Air Force One intercepted by Cuban fighters and forced to reverse course this afternoon. The White House has not issued a statement.

press.source: Radio Habana Cuba, 3:05 p.m. transcript (CIA translation)
press.headline: Castro: Interception Proves Invasion Intent
press.body: Fidel Castro told listeners the unescorted approach of the American president's aircraft was evidence Washington sought a pretext for war, and called on the Cuban people and the Soviet Union to hold firm against any bargain over the island's defenses.

press.headline: White House Silent on Air Force One Incident
press.body: Correspondents in Washington report the White House has neither confirmed nor denied that the President's aircraft attempted to fly into Cuban airspace this afternoon without military escort.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'The MiG pilots had the closure rate and the altitude to do worse than they did. They chose to force a turn, not a shootdown. That's a data point, not a policy. I want the radar tapes before anyone treats this as a signal from Moscow — Havana is not Moscow.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'You sent the President's own aircraft in naked and they turned it back like it was nothing. That tells the Cubans and the Russians we're not willing to back a threat with force. Hit the SAM sites tonight, before they get the idea they can do this twice.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Jack, you cannot do that again. Dobrynin is still talking to me because he thinks we're rational. If Moscow decides you're flying into Havana on your own authority, they'll assume Washington's chain of command has come apart — and then nobody's channel means anything.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 12:47–2:38 p.m. EST: On presidential order, Air Force One departed Andrews AFB for Havana without military escort or Cuban clearance, intending a direct meeting between President Kennedy and Fidel Castro. Cuban MiG-21s intercepted the aircraft south of Key West at 1:19 p.m. and forced its return; it landed back at Andrews at 2:38 p.m. having never entered Cuban airspace. Castro publicly denounced the approach as evidence of imminent invasion. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressed for an immediate strike on Cuban air defenses and warned in writing of uncontrolled escalation risk. Moscow's assessment of the incident remains unknown.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba and its pilot killed. With the quarantine in force, Soviet missiles still on the island, and no hotline to Moscow, President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly unescorted straight to Havana to meet Castro directly. Cuban MiGs intercepted the aircraft south of Florida and forced it back to Andrews without landing in Cuba; no meeting occurred. Castro publicly called the approach proof of imminent invasion and raised Cuban readiness. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs demanded an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites and warned in writing that another aircraft incident could produce uncontrolled escalation. RFK is alarmed at the unilateral flight and anxious to protect his Dobrynin channel; McNamara is withholding judgment pending intercept data. Moscow's interpretation of the incident is not yet known. The quarantine, the missiles, and the risk of nuclear exchange remain unresolved.
